games.title: Hidden Fortunes
games.verdict: A strong, relatable hook (your salon, Swiggy and coffee money turned into crores) with a nice result card and an image share already built in. What holds it back as the featured game: the screen never says 'tap the cards', the copy promises 'half' but uses the full amount, and on a phone the hero spills sideways and 1.5 MB of logo images load just to decorate sliders.
games.load: ~1.8 MB up front: 61 KB page + a 1 MB logo PNG used as the slider knobs + a 0.5 MB logo PNG in the hero + html2canvas (~200 KB); 50 large emoji float behind the page non-stop
games.share_idea: Already has a WhatsApp button; sharpen its text to: 'My ₹10,000 a month of Swiggy + coffee could be ₹3.5 Cr in 30 years (at an assumed 12%). What are YOUR habits worth? 👉 games.investingformummies.com/hidden-fortunes' and point it at the clean /hidden-fortunes link instead of /hidden-fortunes-2.html.
games.share_moment: Result screen, directly under the big 'X× what you put in' panel, before the Download button.

items.text: The intro and tip both say 'what if even half went into a SIP?' but the total uses the full amount of every habit picked; either halve the total or change the words to 'what if this money went into a SIP', so the promise matches the maths.

On first load nothing is selected and the Reveal button is greyed out with no hint why; add a short line like 'Tap the habits you spend on 👇' (or pre-select two cards) so a WhatsApp visitor knows what to do in the first 3 seconds.

On a 375px phone the hero subtitle runs off the right edge and the page scrolls sideways; let the subtitle wrap and hide the 'Scan to Play' QR button on phones (people are already on their phone, so a QR code is useless there and steals the most valuable space).
The slider knobs use a 1 MB round-logo picture and the hero uses a 0.5 MB logo; swap both for small (under 25 KB) versions so the homepage's featured game opens fast on mobile data.

The sliders go from ₹0 to ₹1–3 lakh a month in ₹1,000 steps, so on a phone the knob barely moves between ₹2,000 and ₹6,000; cap each slider at a realistic monthly spend (say ₹20,000–₹50,000) or add –/+ buttons so mums can set their real number.

The 50 big floating emoji keep moving behind the results and sit under the 'Redirect ₹10,000/month…' sentence, making it hard to read; slow them down and fade them out once the result is shown (this also saves phone battery).

Add one honest 'in today's money' line under the 30-year figure (e.g. '₹3.5 Cr in 2056 buys roughly what ₹60 L buys today at 6% inflation'); it keeps the wow but makes the lesson trustworthy and links naturally to the Inflation Calculator.
Let the player choose how long (10/20/30 years) or what share to redirect (25/50/100%) on the result screen, so they can play with it again instead of only 'Try Different Habits'.
Drop '2.0' from the title ('Hidden Fortunes 2.0' means nothing to a first-time visitor) and use one name everywhere: page title, hero and share text.
The habit cards are tap-only boxes, not real buttons, so keyboard and screen-reader users cannot select them; make each card a proper button that announces 'selected'.

After the result, add a gentle line such as 'Want to know where a SIP actually goes and how to start one? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com; right now the result ends with only Reset.

games.title: 3 Buckets
games.verdict: Beautiful buckets, satisfying fly-in animations and genuinely useful 'why this bucket' explanations. What holds it back: it downloads about 6 MB before you can play, and on a phone the three buckets are stacked one under another so you scroll on every single item.
games.load: ~6.3 MB up front: 2.6 MB autoplaying hero video + three 0.65 MB bucket PNGs + a 1 MB round-logo PNG (shown at 28–40px) + a 0.5 MB wide logo that loads and is immediately thrown away + 150 KB marble texture
games.share_idea: 'I scored 11/12 sorting money into Emergency, Stability and Growth buckets 🪣 Can you beat me? 👉 games.investingformummies.com/3-buckets'
games.share_moment: Final screen, right under the score ring and 'Bucket Master!' title.

items.text: Why it is 4.5–6 MB: the decorative hero video (2.6 MB, 1280×720 with a sound track it never plays) autoplays on arrival, each bucket picture is a 650 KB PNG shown at about 230px wide, and two logo PNGs total 1.5 MB; shrink the buckets to ~40 KB WebP each, use small logos, and show only the 60 KB poster image on phones (play the video, re-encoded under 500 KB with no audio, only on desktop) to get the page under 500 KB.

On a phone the buckets stack vertically (Growth starts about 1,100px down, below the fold), so the item and the right bucket are never on screen together and the fly-in animation happens off-screen; put the three buckets side by side as smaller tiles (or as three big labelled buttons) directly under the item card.

Items name real brands as examples (SBI savings account; Reliance, TCS, HDFC Bank inside the Nifty item; L&T and Mahindra for bonds); replace them with generic wording ('a bank savings account', 'India's 50 biggest companies') so nothing reads like a recommendation.

Rates are stated as current facts (PPF ~7.1%, Sukanya ~8.2%, savings ~2.7%, Nifty '12–14%'); add 'rates as of <month/year>' and change the Nifty line to 'has historically… not guaranteed', since these change every quarter.
The government has stopped issuing new Sovereign Gold Bonds, so a mum can no longer act on that item; swap it for 'Gold ETF / Gold mutual fund' or reword it as 'gold held for 8+ years'.

The '🏠 Back to Main Menu' button just restarts this game's own start screen instead of going to the games page, and the start screen promises '🏆 Earn badges' but there are no badges; fix the button's destination and remove or deliver the badges.

The final screen says 'discuss with your group before playing again' — leftover classroom wording; for a solo player say something like 'Tap any item to see why it belongs there' or 'Play again — the items change each time'.
A wrong answer takes about 3 seconds of animation before the explanation pops up, then needs a tap, for each of 12 items; cut the wait to about 1 second so the pace stays snappy on a phone.

The pop-up and item text use projector-sized fonts (set for classroom screens) which make the 'why' box long on a phone; use smaller sizes under 600px wide so the Next button stays visible without scrolling.

Only one item (Sukanya) ever has two right answers; add one or two more genuinely 'it depends' items (e.g. a hybrid fund) so the 'tricky items' promise on the start screen pays off and the game teaches nuance.
The buckets are tap-only pictures, not buttons, so keyboard users cannot play; make each bucket a real button with its name read out.
Under the 'Key Takeaway' on the final screen add a soft 'Want help filling your own three buckets? Find your batch →' link to register.investingformummies.com.

games.title: ₹1 Crore Ladder
games.verdict: A clear guess → reveal → 'cost of waiting' story that lands the compounding lesson well. What holds it back: the answer is spoiled before you guess, the numbers on the page disagree with each other, and on a phone the ladder bars shrink to dots.
games.share_idea: '₹10,000 a month for 25 years → about ₹1.9 Cr at an assumed 12% (I guessed ₹50 L 🙈). How close can you guess? 👉 games.investingformummies.com/one-crore-ladder'
games.share_moment: Right after the ladder finishes (when the ₹1.9 Cr step appears), and again at the end under the 'Cost of Waiting' chart.

items.text: The locked 'One More Question…' card underneath is readable while you are still guessing and says 'You just watched ₹10K/month grow to ₹1.9 Crore'; hide that card's text until it unlocks so the guess is a real guess.

The numbers disagree: the ladder says ₹1.90 Cr at 25 years but the waiting chart shows ₹1.88 Cr for the same 25 years, and the bonus answer says ₹3.53 Cr at 30 years while the chart shows ₹3.49 Cr; use one formula everywhere so a careful mum doesn't lose trust.
Option C ('Over ₹1.5 Crore — compounding is powerful!') gives itself away with its cheerleading tone; make all three options plain numbers so players actually have to think.

The game is called '₹1 Crore Ladder' but never marks the moment you cross ₹1 crore (it happens just after year 20); add a gold '₹1 Crore reached in year 20!' rung or flash — that is the payoff the title promises.

On a phone the 'Growth' bar column in the ladder is squeezed to a dot, and the 'Cost of Waiting' chart is tiny with overlapping 'Returns: ₹6.0…' labels; drop the mini bars on phones and give the chart more height with labels outside the bars.
If you guess wrong, the feedback never tells you the real number ('The answer will surprise you!'); state '₹30 L grows to about ₹1.9 Cr' in the wrong-answer message too.
After the first guess the ladder unlocks but the page doesn't scroll to it, so on a phone it looks like nothing happened; scroll down to the ladder automatically as the later steps already do.
'Start at 25 / 30 / 35' assumes a young player while most Mummies are 30–45; let her enter her own age (or show 30/35/40) so the 'cost of waiting' is about her.
The 12% is labelled 'Expected Return'; call it 'Assumed return (not guaranteed)' on the chips at the top, since the footnote disclaimer is far below.
The hero text sits off-centre to the right because space is reserved for a logo that never appears; remove that left padding or add the logo.
Points are counted in the background but never shown; either show a small '2/2 correct' at the end or remove the scoring so the ending has a clear finish.
Below the 'Emotional Takeaway' add 'Ready to start your own ladder? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com, above Play Again.

games.title: Double or Nothing
games.verdict: A quick, clean 5-round timed quiz that teaches one genuinely handy trick (the Rule of 72). What holds it back: the rules on screen don't match how it actually scores, the right answer is almost always the middle one, and with the same 5 questions every time there is no reason to play twice.
games.load: 124 KB page (mostly unused styles), no libraries; fast
games.share_idea: 'I scored 13/15 on the Rule of 72 speed test ⏱️ — how fast can you tell when your money doubles? 👉 games.investingformummies.com/double-or-nothing'
games.share_moment: Score screen, right under the big score and verdict ('Money Genius!').

items.text: The rules say '15 seconds per round' and '3 pts under 5 sec, 2 pts under 10 sec', but the timer actually runs 30 seconds and gives 3 pts under 10 sec and 2 pts under 20 sec; make the rules and the timer agree.

The correct answer is the middle option in 4 of 5 rounds and the Round 4 answer literally says 'doubles in half the time'; shuffle option order and write neutral options so players must do the 72 ÷ rate sum.
There are only 5 fixed questions, so a replay is identical; add a pool of 15–20 (different rates, prices doubling, 'what rate do I need to double in 6 years?') and pick 5 at random each time.

Round 5 names a real index ('Nifty 50 index fund earning 14% per year') and says it 'has historically returned ~14%' so 'your money doubles roughly every 5 years'; use a generic 'equity fund at an assumed 12%' and add 'past returns are not guaranteed'.
Round 1's 9% FD is higher than any bank FD a mum will see today; use realistic rates (7% FD) so the example feels real, and mention once that the rule is an approximation.
The formula hint is shown on every round, so it's a reading test, not a memory test; show it in rounds 1–2, then hide it behind a 'Need a hint?' tap that costs a point.

The name 'Double or Nothing' suggests a gamble (risking everything), which is the opposite of the lesson; consider 'When Will It Double?' or add a gentle 'double or nothing' bonus round that matches the name.
The finish is a list of rounds; end on a personal punchline instead, e.g. 'Your ₹1 lakh FD at 7% doubles in ~10 years; at 12% in ~6 years', with an input for her own amount.
The hero text sits off-centre to the right because space is reserved for a logo that never appears; remove that left padding or add the logo.
On the score screen add 'Want to learn where your money can actually double faster? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com.

games.title: The Rice & the Chessboard
games.verdict: A lovely, light (24 KB) retelling of a classic story with great 'sack → truck → warehouse' milestones and a strong ending. What holds it back: the story itself is never told up front, on a phone the Next button is below the screen so every tap needs a scroll, and two of the ending's 'wow' facts are wrong.
games.load: 24 KB page, no libraries; very fast
games.share_idea: 'One grain of rice, doubled 64 times, is more rice than the world grows in 900 years 🌾 Now imagine your money doing that. 👉 games.investingformummies.com/rice-and-chessboard'
games.share_moment: End screen ('The King Ran Out of Rice'), under the 'So what does this mean for your money?' box.

items.text: The story (a wise man asks the king for 1 grain on the first square, doubled on every square) is never explained before you start; add a 2-line intro card with the deal and a 'Do you accept?' button so the player knows what is being promised.

On a phone the 'Next Square' button sits about 950px down, below the screen, so each tap means scrolling down and the board scrolls out of view; pin the Next / Auto-play buttons to the bottom of the screen on phones.

Two ending facts are wrong: 460 billion tonnes of rice is LESS than a single big mountain, not 'more than every mountain range in India', and 8 billion people eating 200 g a day would get through it in about 790 years, not 'over 2,000 years'; correct or replace these cards.

The ending says 'good Indian index funds have averaged 12–15% a year for decades' as a fact; soften to 'equity has historically returned around 12% (not guaranteed)' and label the ₹10,000 → ₹12.8 L example as an assumption.
Add a quick prediction before play ('Which square fills a whole sack of rice?' or 'Would you take this deal or ₹1 crore?') so the player has something at stake when the numbers explode.

The big counter switches to Western words (Million, Billion, Quintillion) and the board shows '10^15', while the milestones use lakh and crore; use lakh/crore (or 'crore crore') consistently and drop the '10^' notation — Mummies think in lakhs.
The numbers inside the squares are about 6px tall on a phone and unreadable; show them only on bigger screens and let the big counter and milestone text carry the story on mobile.
The fill bar shows '33%' at square 22 (on a 'log scale') which reads as a third of the rice, when it is a tiny fraction; replace the % with the milestone name ('sack') and drop the 'log scale' label.
It uses a different gold (#f6c842), an all-dark theme and no IFM logo, unlike the other games; bring it onto the brand gold and add the logo so a shared link is recognisably IFM.

After 'Start early.' on the end screen, add 'Want to put the chessboard to work on your own money? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com, and a link to Double or Nothing as the natural next game.

games.title: NAV Pizza
games.verdict: The pizza-slice metaphor is a smart, memorable way to bust the 'low NAV = cheap fund' myth, and the explanations are excellent. What holds it back: it is one very long page (about 8½ phone screens) with nine questions, no progress counter and no ending, and the right answer is usually the longest, most sensible-sounding option.
games.load: 143 KB page, no libraries; fast to load but a 6,900px-long page on a phone
games.share_idea: 'Quick test: Fund A's NAV is ₹20, Fund B's is ₹100 — which is cheaper? 🍕 I got 8/9 on the NAV myth quiz. 👉 games.investingformummies.com/nav-pizza'
games.share_moment: A new end card after the last question showing her score (e.g. '8/9 myths busted').

items.text: There is no ending — after question 9 nothing happens, and the points are counted but never shown; add a final card with her score, the three key lessons (NAV ≠ price tag, dividends come out of NAV, dips mean more units) and Play Again.
All nine questions sit on one long page with greyed-out cards below; show one question at a time with a '3 of 9' progress bar so a phone player knows how far she has to go.

The correct answer is almost always the longest, most balanced-sounding option (C or B); rewrite options to similar lengths and vary where the right one sits, so players learn rather than spot the pattern.

In View 2 the ₹100 fund is simply given the higher return, which can leave a beginner thinking 'higher NAV = better'; add a one-line flip ('…and if the ₹20 fund had earned 15%, it would win — the NAV never decides') to close that loophole.

The hero puts white text on a pale gold background, which is hard to read in sunlight, and sits off-centre because of space reserved for a missing logo; use the navy or a darker gold behind the title and centre it.
Use today's term 'IDCW (formerly Dividend) plan' in the dividend questions, because that is what a mum will see on her fund app and statement.
Fix the garbled sentence 'The total value stayed ₹1,000 at the start' in View 1 (e.g. 'Both started at ₹1,000 and both ended at ₹1,100').
Both 'pizzas' are the same emoji, so the visual doesn't show the idea; draw Fund A as a pizza cut into 50 thin slices and Fund B into 10 big ones — same pizza, different slicing.
The card titled 'Now That You Know the Truth About NAV…' looks like the last question but five more follow; retitle it so the structure doesn't feel endless.
On the new end card add 'Want to read a fund factsheet with confidence? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com.

games.title: Radha's Money Mission
games.verdict: A relatable 'help a working mum' case study with a good variety of question types (calculate, match, choose). What holds it back: real fund names presented as the 'perfect' pick, a replay bug that makes the game freeze at question 3, and it opens with the hardest maths question.
games.load: 132 KB page + Chart.js (~200 KB) that the game never uses
games.share_idea: 'I helped Radha (32, Mumbai) sort out her mutual funds and scored 95/120 ⭐ Can you be a Gold Star Mum? 👉 games.investingformummies.com/radhas-mission'
games.share_moment: 'Mission Complete!' screen, under the score ring and badges.

items.text: Questions name real funds — 'HDFC Balanced Advantage Fund… 25% returns last year', 'Axis Long Term Equity', 'HDFC Mid-Cap Opportunities', 'SBI Small Cap' — and call each the 'perfect fund' for a friend; replace with made-up fund houses (e.g. 'Sunrise Small Cap Fund') so it can't read as a recommendation.

After 'Try Again', tapping any answer on questions 3, 4, 6 and 7 does nothing (verified in the browser), so a replaying player gets stuck at question 3; the same fault means the 'Concept Queen' badge can never be earned — fix how those questions remember they were answered.

Question 4 teaches 'always choose Direct, the RM ticks Regular for commission', but question 8's 'correct' answer puts a retired mum in a Regular-plan mid-cap fund for income; change Deepa's mum's answer (or the wording) so the game doesn't contradict itself and doesn't steer a retiree into mid-caps.

The very first question is a 3-step NAV calculation with odd numbers (₹850, 40 units) typed into boxes; start with an easy confidence-builder (the SIP or Regular-vs-Direct question) and move the maths to the middle.
The points don't add up: question 2 can give at most 18 (labelled 20) and question 5 gives 16 (labelled 15), so the advertised 120 is impossible; correct the labels or the scoring.
The number boxes use small text, so iPhones zoom the whole page in when you tap them; make the answer boxes at least 16px text and bring up the number keypad.
When a question is answered the next one unlocks quietly below without scrolling; scroll to it (as other games do) so phone players know to continue.

'Amisha' appears in questions 4 and 6 with no introduction, and the intro's daughter, goal and ₹2 lakh bonus are never used; introduce Amisha as Radha's friend/adviser in the intro and use the ₹2 lakh in at least one question.
The ELSS answer says 'save income tax this year'; add 'under the old tax regime', because under the new regime 80C does not apply and many mums are now on it.
Question 3 contains its own answer ('invest a fixed amount every month automatically is called… SIP'); make it a real scenario so it's worth 10 points.
Remove the Chart.js library it loads but never uses (~200 KB).
On 'Mission Complete!' add 'Radha learned this in an IFM batch — find yours →' linking to register.investingformummies.com; it fits the story perfectly.

games.title: The Three Investors
games.verdict: A dramatic, well-told comparison of SIP vs lump sum vs market timing with a nice ranked reveal. What holds it back: the player never makes a decision — 'your' strategy is picked at random and auto-played — and 1 time in 5 the random pick wins and the game congratulates you for timing the market.
games.share_idea: Already has a WhatsApp button but it links to the www homepage; change it to: 'I tried to time the market against a steady SIP over 12 years 📉📈 — SIP still won (₹21 L vs my ₹16 L). Think you can beat it? 👉 games.investingformummies.com/three-investors'
games.share_moment: Big Reveal screen, directly under the three ranked result cards.

items.text: Let the player actually be the market timer: show each year's price move and let her tap 'Invest ₹1L / ₹2L / ₹4L' or 'Wait', then compare her result with the SIP and lump-sum friends — right now she just watches a random preset and is labelled 'You'.

One of the five random presets ('The Brave Buyer') wins with ₹29.5 L and the message says 'You timed the market perfectly'; until the player makes real choices, remove that preset or present it clearly as 'what a lucky hindsight timer would have got'.
The WhatsApp share sends people to the www homepage instead of this game, so friends never land on it; link to games.investingformummies.com/three-investors and include the player's result.

The year-by-year autoplay scrolls the page for you every second for about 15 seconds, fighting the player's thumb; let her step through with a 'Next year' button (or only auto-scroll if she hasn't touched the screen).

The lesson implies SIP always beats a lump sum, but here that only happens because the market crashes right after year 1; add one honest line ('in a steadily rising market the lump sum usually wins — SIP wins on discipline and peace of mind').
On a phone each result card is about 250px tall so the three cards fill more than a screen; show them as a compact side-by-side row or a single ranked list so the comparison is visible at a glance.
The hero text sits off-centre to the right because space is reserved for a logo that never appears; remove that left padding or add the logo.
Under the lesson box add 'Want a SIP plan you can stick to? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com.

games.title: Inflation Calculator
games.verdict: Three genuinely useful views (future monthly expense, buying power, corpus needed) with clean result cards on desktop. What holds it back: it is slow because the phone has to download and run a 2.8 MB code translator before anything appears, and on a phone the layout is broken — the amount box is 28px wide and the tabs are cut off.
games.load: 347 KB page (only about a fifth is this calculator; the rest is code for three retired apps) + React + Babel in-browser compiler (2.8 MB unpacked, ~1 MB download) that must run before the tool shows; mobile Lighthouse 34
games.share_idea: 'My ₹40,000 monthly household budget will be ₹71,600 in 10 years at 6% inflation 😳 Check yours: 👉 games.investingformummies.com/inflation-calculator'
games.share_moment: Under the big result number in each tab (e.g. 'In year 10 your monthly expense will be ₹17,908').

items.text: Why it scores 34: the calculator is hidden inside a frame that only starts after the page loads, then downloads React plus the Babel translator and converts the code on the phone before showing anything; pre-build it once into plain JavaScript (as planned for the other Babel games) so it appears almost instantly.
About 270 KB of the page is leftover code and styles for other apps (Investopia, Lifestyle Time Machine, 3 Buckets styles) that this page never shows; delete it so the page is a fraction of its size.

On a 375px phone the ₹ amount box is only 28px wide so '10,000' is invisible, the third tab ('Corpus Calculator') and 'yrs → 2036' are cut off, and the page has 28px side margins inside another padded box; stack the controls full-width and shrink the tab labels on phones.

'Total corpus required' simply adds up every future year's expenses and assumes the money earns nothing while you draw it down, which overstates what a mum needs; either add an assumed return (with the assumption shown) or rename it 'Total you will spend over N years'.

The tip 'Equity mutual funds averaging 12–14% p.a. are one of India's most powerful inflation hedges' states returns as fact; reword to 'equity has historically returned more than inflation over long periods (not guaranteed)'.

Start with a familiar example: the code already has a 'basket' of everyday items (coffee, petrol, onions, rice) that is never shown; use it ('your ₹60 kilo of rice will cost ₹107 in 10 years') — it lands harder than percentages.
The hero labels it 'Resource' and sits off-centre with space reserved for a missing logo; centre it and give it the same look as the game heroes so it feels part of the set.
The 'Rule of 72' box actually shows an exact calculation, not the rule; call it 'Your money's buying power halves in…' so beginners aren't confused by the label.
Under the 'To beat inflation' box add 'Want a plan that beats inflation? Find your batch →' linking to register.investingformummies.com — this is the most natural lead-in of all the tools.
